issues.description: The stated formula for type diagnosticity is mathematically incorrect given the reported example values. The text says diagnosticity is computed by dividing the number of words with a suffix in a category by 'the total number of words falling into this category' (i.e., all nouns/adjectives/verbs in the lexicon). However, applying this formula to the –IAN example would yield a tiny fraction (e.g., ~136 IAN-nouns / ~50,000 total nouns), not 0.54 as stated. The actual denominator—consistent with all values in Appendix A—must be the total number of words containing that suffix (regardless of category), making this a conditional probability P(category | suffix). The description reverses numerator and denominator logic, making the methodology irreproducible as written.
issues.quote: type diagnosticity is calculated by dividing the number of words ending in this suffix and falling into this category by the total number of words falling into this category

issues.description: The paper reports that 64 suffixes were excluded from the 154-suffix full set for having fewer than 20 exemplar words, leaving 'the remaining 95 suffixes.' However, 154 − 64 = 90, not 95. This five-suffix discrepancy is unexplained and cannot be reconciled from the text or appendix. It calls into question whether the frequency-filtered analyses were performed on the correctly identified subset and whether the reported stability of mean values across the filtered set is accurate.
issues.quote: we excluded all suffixes that occur in fewer than 20 different words in the CELEX database, i.e. 64 suffixes (Baayen et al., 1993). For the remaining 95 suffixes, the mean diagnosticity and specificity values were virtually unchanged

issues.description: The go-past time congruency effect is reported with B = 41 and t = 3.837 in the results text, but Table 5 reports B = 43 and t = 3.76 for the same effect. These values cannot both be correct. Given that the table presumably reflects the final model output, the in-text reporting appears to contain transcription errors. The magnitude of the discrepancy (B differs by ~5%, t differs by ~2%) is sufficient to raise questions about which values are authoritative, and about the reliability of other numerical reporting throughout.
issues.quote: There was an effect of congruency on go-past time (B = 41, t = 3.837, p < 0.001) ... [Table 5:] Estimate (B) = 43, z/t value = t = 3.76 ***

issues.description: The regressions-out congruency effect is reported with B = 0.3 and z = 3.12 in the results text, but Table 5 reports B = 0.25 and z = 2.65 for the same effect. These values are inconsistent: z = 3.12 gives p ≈ 0.002, while z = 2.65 gives p ≈ 0.008, both nominally p < 0.01 but reflecting meaningfully different effect estimates. The discrepancy undermines confidence in the reported statistics and cannot be resolved without access to the raw model output.
issues.quote: The effect of congruency on regressions-out was significant in the expected direction, i.e. incongruent targets were more likely to elicit regressions to earlier regions of the sentence (B = 0.3, z = 3.12, p < 0.01) ... [Table 5:] Estimate (B) = 0.25, z/t value = z = 2.65 **

issues.description: A z-value of 0.60 is reported with p < 0.01 in the Experiment 2 token-based specificity interaction analysis. A z of 0.60 corresponds to a two-tailed p-value of approximately 0.55 (one-tailed ≈ 0.27). It is mathematically impossible for z = 0.60 to yield p < 0.01. Either the z-value or the p-value is erroneous. This is a consequential error because the token-based analysis is used to contrast with the type-based findings throughout the paper, and an incorrect statistic changes whether the interaction was significant at all.
issues.quote: the interaction between specificity and condition was significant, such that the target spelling became used more often in the congruent condition than in the incongruent condition as its specificity increased (B = 1.9, z = 2.8, p < 0.01; for the token analyses - z = 0.60, p < 0.01)

issues.description: The generalised mixed model for Experiment 1 includes only a random intercept for subjects and no random effect for items (suffixes or nonwords). With only 20 suffixes (10 per category, each appearing twice per participant across a between-list design), suffixes are effectively treated as fixed rather than random. This violates the by-items random effects requirement in psycholinguistics (Clark, 1973; Barr et al., 2013) and can substantially inflate Type I error rates. The same issue applies to Experiment 2, where 'analyses were otherwise identical to those in Experiment 1.' Experiment 3 explicitly adds a random intercept for suffixes, suggesting the authors were aware of this requirement but omitted it in Experiments 1 and 2.
issues.quote: This analysis was expressed in the model glmer (response ~ condition + (1|subject), data, family = "binomial").

issues.description: Six eye-movement measures are tested independently in Experiment 3 (word-skipping, first fixation duration, first run dwell time, go-past time, regressions-in, regressions-out), with no correction for family-wise error rate. At α = 0.05, the probability of at least one false positive across six independent tests exceeds 26%. Subsequently, follow-up diagnosticity × congruency interactions are tested only for the two measures that reached significance (go-past and regressions-out), creating a two-stage selection process that further inflates Type I error without acknowledgment. No Bonferroni, FDR, or other correction is applied or even discussed.
issues.quote: we chose to monitor a variety of typically studied measures (that characterise skips, fixations, reading time, and regressions; see Rayner et al., 2004; Warren et al., 2009)

issues.description: A statistically significant difference in the number of pre-target words exists between congruent and incongruent conditions in Experiment 3 (4.75 vs. 5.23 words; t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05). Pre-target sentence length can affect reading time on target words through syntactic wrap-up and preview effects. Although post-target regions and letter counts are matched, the word count difference is acknowledged but dismissed without correction or covariate adjustment. This is particularly concerning for measures like go-past time, which integrates across re-reading of earlier sentence regions—exactly the measure showing the critical congruency effect.
issues.quote: Note that the number of words pre-target was slightly different across conditions (congruent: 4.75, incongruent: 5.23, t(64) = 2.07, p < 0.05).

issues.description: The stated theoretical predictions are inverted relative to both theoretical logic and the actual experimental operationalizations. The text predicts that diagnosticity (spelling→meaning consistency) will affect spelling production tasks, and that specificity (meaning→spelling consistency) will affect reading/categorization tasks. However, diagnosticity—the probability of a category given a spelling—is most directly relevant when going from spelling to meaning (reading), while specificity—the probability of a spelling given meaning+phonology—is most directly relevant when going from meaning to spelling (spelling production). The experiments themselves correctly test diagnosticity in Experiments 1 and 3 (reading/categorization) and specificity in Experiment 2 (spelling), which is the opposite mapping to the stated prediction. The mismatch between the stated hypothesis and the experimental design leaves the theoretical rationale confused.
issues.quote: we hypothesise that diagnosticity, a measure of spelling-to-meaning consistency, would impact on tasks that involve the production of spelling, while specificity, a measure of meaning-to-spelling consistency, would impact on tasks involving the mapping of print to meaning (i.e. semantic categorisation, reading)

issues.description: The graded diagnosticity analysis in Experiment 1 involves multiplying diagnosticity by −1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes before entering it into the model. This sign-flip transformation is applied post-hoc after the categorical condition effect is established, and is described as a check rather than a pre-planned analysis. The transformation conflates adjective-high and noun-low ends of a single continuous scale, which could artificially amplify the apparent correlation between diagnosticity and response pattern. No rationale for choosing this specific transformation over alternatives (e.g., bipolar coding, separate models) is provided.
issues.quote: In order to investigate this statistically, we multiplied our diagnosticity measure by -1 for noun-diagnostic suffixes and substituted this measure in our model, in place of the condition variable.

issues.description: In Experiment 3, the diagnosticity × congruency interaction is only tested and reported for the two eye-movement measures that showed a significant main effect of congruency (go-past time and regressions-out). It is unclear whether this interaction was tested for all six measures and selectively reported, or was pre-planned only for the significant measures. This selective follow-up is a form of researcher degrees of freedom: if the interaction had been tested for all six measures with any pattern of significance, the reported results would represent a subset chosen based on the main effect outcome, inflating Type I error for the interaction tests as well.
issues.quote: Further analyses investigated whether the size of the congruency effects on the go-past and regressions-out measures was influenced by the degree to which suffix spellings were diagnostic of lexical category.

issues.description: None of the three experiments are described as pre-registered. The study involves multiple dependent variables (6 eye-movement measures in Experiment 3), multiple analytic models (type vs. token diagnosticity/specificity, graded vs. categorical versions), and multiple follow-up tests conducted conditionally on main effect significance. Without pre-registration, the reader cannot distinguish confirmatory from exploratory analyses. The OSF link provided contains data and analyses, but no pre-registration document is mentioned or linked. This is especially concerning given the exploratory nature of the diagnosticity × congruency interaction tests.
issues.quote: We did not have any concrete predictions as to which eye-movement measures would be affected by the diagnosticity manipulation, so we chose to monitor a variety of typically studied measures

issues.description: The paper does not explicitly state that different participants were used across the three experiments, despite all being run at the same institution with similar recruitment procedures. If participants overlapped between experiments—particularly between Experiment 1 and Experiment 3, which use the same nonwords and some identical sentence frames—prior exposure would constitute a substantial confound. Experiment 3 participants would have already categorized the nonwords in Experiment 1 and potentially also spelled them in Experiment 2, creating familiarity effects that could enhance or alter the observed congruency effects.
issues.quote: 47 undergraduate students at Royal Holloway University of London were recruited following the same procedure as in Experiments 1 and 2.

issues.description: No sample size justification or power analysis is reported for any of the three experiments. Experiment 2 has only 29 participants with 11 suffixes and a within-subjects design; Experiment 1 has 46 participants split across two between-subjects lists with only 2 observations per suffix per participant per list. The graded diagnosticity/specificity analyses—which are the theoretically central claims—require sufficient power to detect suffix-level interactions with continuous predictors, but no justification is provided that these sample sizes are adequate for such analyses.
issues.quote: Participants were 29 undergraduate students from Royal Holloway University of London.

issues.description: No standardized effect sizes (Cohen's d, η², R², odds ratios, or Nagelkerke R² for logistic models) are reported for any of the analyses across all three experiments or the computational analysis. Reporting only B, z, and t values with p-values makes it impossible to evaluate the practical significance of the effects or to use these results for power calculations or meta-analysis. This is particularly important for the graded diagnosticity/specificity effects, where the slope coefficients need context to assess their psychological importance.
issues.quote: Results showed a main effect of suffix condition such that noun-diagnostic suffixes elicited more "noun" responses (B = -1.57, z = -4.224, p < 0.0001)

issues.description: Experiment 1 has 11.7% of data points missing due to timeouts or non-corresponding button presses, which is a substantial exclusion rate. The paper reports this figure but provides no analysis of whether missingness is systematically related to experimental condition (adjective vs. noun suffix), suffix diagnosticity, or any other variable. If, for example, participants timed out more frequently on weakly diagnostic suffixes, the graded diagnosticity effect—the key finding—could be artefactually inflated by selective retention of high-confidence, high-diagnosticity trials.
issues.quote: We used generalised mixed modelling analysis from the lme4 package in R (Bates et al., 2014) on 1,625 data points (11.7% of data points were missing due to timeouts or button presses that did not correspond to a response).

issues.description: Comprehension accuracy in Experiment 3 is reported as '0.86%' ranging from '0.66% to 0.98%.' These cannot be percentages (0.86% would be near-chance performance, and ranges of 0.66%–0.98% are implausible on a binary forced-choice task). The values are clearly proportions (0.86, 0.66, 0.98), and the percent sign is misplaced throughout. This is not merely a formatting issue: if taken literally, accuracy of 0.86% would indicate that the comprehension check was essentially non-functional, undermining the claim that participants were engaged with sentence meaning during reading.
issues.quote: Average accuracy on comprehension trials was 0.86% (ranging from 0.66% to 0.98%).

issues.description: When testing the diagnosticity interaction for regressions-out, the text states 'when the interaction was added: Chi (2) = 14.37, p < 0.001,' reporting df = 2. However, the text specifies only 'the interaction' was added (not also the main effect of diagnosticity as was done for the go-past model). Adding a single interaction term to a model should yield a chi-square test with df = 1, not df = 2. This discrepancy suggests either the wrong df is reported or an additional term was also added but not mentioned, making the model comparison non-transparent.
issues.quote: The fit of regressions-out model improved significantly when the interaction was added: Chi (2) = 14.37, p < 0.001.

issues.description: The paper repeatedly makes causal and teleological claims about English spelling having 'evolved' or 'become fractionated' to 'maximise the transmission of meaningful information.' The primary evidence for this—Berg and Aronoff's (2017) diachronic data showing that spelling variants for /əs/ narrowed over time—is consistent with the claim but does not establish that maximizing meaning transmission was the selective pressure. Spelling changes could reflect scribal conventions, printing standardization, Latinate borrowing patterns, or many other processes. Framing this as spelling 'maximising' transmission implies intentional optimization that the data do not support.
issues.quote: English spelling may have become fractionated in such a way that the high degree of spelling-sound inconsistency maximises the transmission of meaningful information in the service of skilled reading.

issues.description: All three experiments used undergraduate students from a single UK university (Royal Holloway, University of London). The paper draws broad conclusions about 'skilled readers' and their long-term knowledge of the English writing system, but the sample is demographically homogeneous (WEIRD: Western, Educated, Industrialized, Rich, Democratic) and may not represent the full range of reading skill, age, or educational background. The General Discussion makes no acknowledgment of this sampling limitation despite claims that extend to adult skilled readers in general.
issues.quote: We have shown that the average reader learns and subsequently relies on morphological cues to class even without explicit instruction to do so

issues.description: The computational analysis restricts to three lexical categories (nouns, adjectives, verbs) while omitting adverbs, despite adverbs being formed by the most frequent derivational suffix in the dataset (+LY, type frequency = 2,717, the highest of any suffix). The consequence is that +LY and +ALLY (frequency = 397) are included in the 154-suffix dataset but have near-zero diagnosticity across all three categories (e.g., +LY: 0.039/0.006/0.002), dragging down mean diagnosticity values while being substantively uninformative. The reported mean diagnosticity of 0.78 is misleading because it averages over suffixes whose near-zero values are artefacts of category exclusion rather than genuine ambiguity. The claim that derivational suffixes are 'ubiquitously' diagnostic cannot be defended without including adverbs.
issues.quote: Our analyses consider three major lexical categories: nouns, adjectives, and verbs.

issues.description: The entropy regression analysis comparing spelling versus phonological predictability reports an F-test to evaluate whether the regression slope differs from 1.0, but provides only one degree of freedom parameter: 'F (1) = 7.44, p < 0.01.' The denominator degrees of freedom are omitted entirely. Without knowing the residual df, it is impossible to evaluate the test statistic or verify the p-value. Additionally, the confidence interval for the slope estimate (0.9, SE = 0.04) is not accompanied by the sample size used in this regression (n = 154 or a filtered subset), making the test non-reproducible.
issues.quote: We found that the regression line has a slope of 0.9 (SE = 0.04, t = 25.32, p < 0.0001), and that this slope is significantly different from 1 (F (1) = 7.44, p < 0.01).

issues.description: Four out of six eye-movement measures in Experiment 3 show null effects of congruency (skipping, first fixation duration, first run dwell time, regressions-in). These null results are interpreted as evidence that spelling-category incongruence affects later integration processes but not early lexical processing. However, no Bayes factors, equivalence tests, or sensitivity analyses are provided to quantify the strength of evidence for these nulls. Without such analyses, readers cannot distinguish genuine null effects from underpowered tests, which is critical because the interpretation of which processing stage is affected depends entirely on the null results being true nulls.
issues.quote: There was no effect of congruency on skipping behaviour... There was no effect of congruency on first fixation durations... There was no effect of congruency on the first run dwell time... There was no effect of congruency on this measure.
